title: Dr. Jitendra Singh Inaugurates BSL-3 Facility at CSIR-CDRI Lucknow; Says India Moving Towards Becoming a Global Hub for Innovative Drug Discovery and Development
subtitle:
New BSL-3/ABSL-3 Facility at CSIR-CDRI Lucknow to Strengthen India's Research Capabilities Against Challenging Infectious Diseases: Dr. Jitendra Singh
CDRI Has Developed 13 Drugs That Have Reached the Market, Licensed Over 80 Process Technologies and Filed More Than 1,000 Patents: Dr. Jitendra Singh
India's Pharmaceutical Sector Must Move Beyond Generic Drug Manufacturing to Become a Global Discoverer of Innovative Medicines: Dr. Jitendra Singh
Minister Emphasises Industry Partnerships, Artificial Intelligence and Clinical Translation to Accelerate Drug Discovery and Advance Viksit Bharat 2047
body_text: Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Vice President, CSIR, Dr. Jitendra Singh today inaugurated the state-of-the-art Biosafety Level-3 (BSL-3)/Animal Biosafety Level-3 (ABSL-3) Facility and Dr. B. Mukerji Lecture Theatre at CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow, and hailed India’s health innovations saying that India is moving towards becoming a global hub for innovative drug discovery and development. The Minister said that the country must now move beyond its established position as a major global supplier of generic medicines and emerge as a discoverer and developer of innovative therapeutics, with indigenous research, clinical development and industry partnerships playing a critical role in this transition. This shift, he said, is essential for strengthening India’s pharmaceutical leadership and achieving the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. The programme was attended by Dr. Radha Rangarajan, Director, CSIR-CDRI; Dr. Prabodh K. Trivedi, Director, CSIR-CIMAP; former Director of CSIR-CDRI Dr. Madhu Dikshit; representatives of ICMR–National Institute of Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur; Uttar Pradesh University of Medical Sciences, Saifai; and Medanta Hospital, Lucknow, besides scientists, researchers, students, technical and non-technical staff and industry representatives. The newly inaugurated BSL-3/ABSL-3 facility will provide high-containment research infrastructure for scientific studies involving Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), strengthening the Institute’s capabilities in research on challenging infectious diseases. Dr. Jitendra Singh also congratulated CSIR-CDRI on the collaborative agreements signed with ICMR–National Institute of Research in Tribal Health, Uttar Pradesh University of Medical Sciences and Medanta Hospital, expressing confidence that these partnerships would lead to fruitful collaborative research programmes, accelerate clinical translation and deliver measurable benefits to society. The Minister said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, science, technology and innovation have become central to India’s national development, with a strong emphasis on research that addresses citizens’ needs and delivers tangible solutions. He cited CSIR-CDRI’s journey from drug discovery and clinical development to diagnostics, process technologies and affordable healthcare interventions as an example of how scientific research can translate into meaningful public benefit. CSIR-CDRI has developed 13 drugs that have reached the market, licensed more than 80 process technologies and six diagnostic technologies, published over 12,000 research articles and filed more than 456 international patents and 586 patents in India. Its research infrastructure includes a compound library of approximately 90,000 molecules, more than 50 animal models and over 30 in-vitro screening systems, alongside advanced analytical instrumentation, GLP-certified toxicology and safety pharmacology facilities and specialised cardiac safety assessment infrastructure. Referring to CDRI’s contribution to public healthcare, Dr. Jitendra Singh cited Centchroman, also known as Ormeloxifene, an indigenous non-steroidal, once-a-week oral contraceptive developed by the Institute. Its inclusion in the National Family Planning Programme in 2016 marked an important milestone in translating indigenous scientific research into a public health intervention. More than 350 lakh strips have been distributed free of cost to women across the country through ASHA workers during the last five years, with the current user base exceeding five lakh women. The Minister also referred to CDRI’s promising drug-development pipeline, including a standardised extract of Picrorhiza kurroa for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, now referred to as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), which has completed Phase III clinical trials. Two other compounds discovered at CDRI, L-Ormeloxifene for contraception and S007-1500 for fracture healing, have entered Phase I clinical trials. The Institute is also pursuing advanced research leads for malaria, cancer, neuropathic pain and age-related macular degeneration, along with phytopharmaceutical candidates for cancer and Parkinson’s disease. Dr. Jitendra Singh said India ranks third globally in pharmaceutical production by volume and 11 th by value and is among the world’s largest suppliers of generic medicines, meeting over 50 per cent of Africa’s generic medicine requirements and approximately 40 per cent of the generic drug demand in the United States. While appreciating the achievements of India’s pharmaceutical industry, he said the next phase of growth must involve moving up the value chain, from predominantly manufacturing generic medicines to discovering and developing innovative therapeutics. He said drug discovery and development are complex, expensive and high-risk endeavours requiring sustained investment and long-term commitment. National research institutions must pursue cutting-edge science, explore novel targets and mechanisms and generate robust proof-of-concept data, while pharmaceutical companies should be encouraged to take promising discoveries forward through further development, clinical evaluation and commercialisation. Stronger technology-transfer mechanisms and early industry participation can create an effective pathway from laboratory research to patients. Appreciating CDRI’s ongoing collaborations with Zydus, Cipla, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Himalaya, Themis Medicare and several startups, the Minister encouraged the Institute to further strengthen its role as a research and innovation partner for the pharmaceutical industry. Calling for greater adoption of emerging technologies, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the integration of biology, chemistry, computational sciences and artificial intelligence offers tremendous opportunities to transform drug discovery. He encouraged scientists to pursue ambitious research questions, embrace out-of-the-box ideas and work closely with clinicians, hospitals and industry partners to ensure that research remains aligned with actual clinical requirements. At every stage of drug discovery and development, the ultimate beneficiary must be the patient, he said. The Minister also appreciated CDRI’s contribution to scientific capacity building, with the Institute having trained more than 2,000 PhDs and over 10,000 trainees. He said skilled researchers, technologists and regulatory specialists are indispensable to a strong innovation ecosystem and that the contribution of CDRI-trained professionals across academia, startups, industry and research organisations represents a valuable national investment. Dr. Jitendra Singh expressed confidence that CSIR-CDRI would continue to strengthen India’s capabilities in indigenous drug discovery and contribute significantly to the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Quoting former President Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, he said, “Dream, dream, dream. Dreams transform into thoughts and thoughts result in action.” He encouraged the scientific community to dream big, translate scientific ideas into discoveries and develop medicines that improve and save lives. ***** SG/AK
